turns.en: All you have to do is visit athleticgreens.com/lenny. Again, that's athleticgreens.com/lenny. Take ownership over your health and pick up the ultimate daily nutritional insurance. Just to set context, most of your experience is B2B, so I guess we should just let people know this is probably mostly B2B advice.
turns.zh: 你唯一要做的，就是访问 athleticgreens.com/lenny。再说一遍，是 athleticgreens.com/lenny。把健康的主导权拿回自己手里，备上终极的每日营养保险。说句背景，你大部分经验是 B2B 的，所以我想我们该让大家知道，这大概主要都是 B2B 的建议。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Sorry. Yes, mostly B2B advice. I think a lot of this holds, I think the fuel engine stuff holds for B2C. I think the roles pretty much hold, but you might hear the word brand marketing thrown out a lot more in B2C and that's what we're going to be talking about, the fuel stuff and maybe that's going to be what they hire before they hire say like a product marketer. But it's kind of the same set of functions. But most of my experience are B2B and most of the startups I work with are B2B, but some of it holds.
turns.zh: 抱歉。对，主要是 B2B 建议。我觉得很多内容都成立，燃料引擎那套在 B2C 也成立。我觉得那些角色基本也成立，但在 B2C 里你可能更多听到"品牌营销"这个词被抛出来，而那就是我们要聊的——燃料那块，也许那会是他们在招产品营销之前先招的东西。但职能集合基本一样。不过我大部分经验是 B2B，我合作的大部分初创也是 B2B，但有一部分也适用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was going to ask about brand marketing, that's like another bucket, right? We haven't talked about that as a type of skill or does that fall into one of these that you've talked about?
turns.zh: 对，我刚想问品牌营销，那是另一个桶对吧？我们还没把它当成一种技能类型聊过，还是说它属于你刚说的某一类里？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: To me, brand marketing is a combination or has some of the work that happens by a product marketer and by a content and community marketer. But maybe they also are more influential on the design side of things. And so brand marketing is another one that needs 75 different things. Sometimes it means you literally manage designers or you're a trade up producer, and sometimes it means you are more doing work on what are the stories that we're trying to tell and you're doing more of the content stuff. And sometimes it means I'm doing the positioning work, sometimes it means I'm working on the website or branded paid stuff and consumer.
turns.zh: 对我来说，品牌营销是产品营销和内容/社区营销做的部分工作的组合。但也许他们在设计那一侧的影响力更大。所以品牌营销也是一个需要很多不同东西的领域。有时它意味着你字面意义上管理设计师、或者你更像是个监制，有时它意味着你更多在做"我们要讲什么故事"这类工作、更多偏内容。有时它意味着我在做定位工作，有时意味着我在搞网站或者品牌付费投放、还有消费端。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So it means a lot of things too. But usually in B2B, the person that kind of owns the brand is the positioning story side of brand is owned by product marketing. And the design side of brand is either just owned by the product designer on first or working with a brand designer or if the marketer has skillset set there could be owned by them as well. So it's a little murky at first, but eventually on B2B teams when I've grown teams plus 10 to 15 people, I'll have a brand person that is working really closely with the designers and kind of making sure that everything that we're producing on the content side of things is up to... They're acting as sort an editor there.
turns.zh: 所以它也意味着很多东西。但在 B2B 里，通常那个拥有品牌的人——品牌里定位故事那一侧——是归产品营销的。而品牌的设计那一侧，要么最早就是归产品设计师的，要么跟品牌设计师协作，或者如果那个市场人员有这块技能，也可以归他们。所以一开始有点模糊，但等 B2B 团队长大到 10 到 15 人，我会有一个品牌的人，跟设计师紧密配合，确保我们在内容侧产出的所有东西都够格……他们在那儿像个编辑。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: They're making sure everything ladders up to the overall story. So they're helping tell the story, they're helping make sure the design is right. And in some instances I'll have a brand person that's kind of working on these larger brand initiatives. We did a huge data study when I was at Carta and the person that kind of ran that whole initiative and the events and it was sort of a separate initiative that had a lot of different parts was my brand marketer. They were kind of working on these larger sort of big data project that's made across all of marketing.
turns.zh: 他们确保一切都能往上接到整体故事线。所以他们在帮着讲故事、帮着确保设计是对的。有些情况下，我会有一个品牌的人在做那些更大的品牌项目。我在 Carta 时做过一个超大的数据研究，那个基本上主导了整个项目、加上各种活动、是个有好多不同组成部分的独立项目的人，就是我的品牌营销。他们当时在做一个横跨整个营销的、更大的大数据项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Well you talked about the growth PM role kind of adjacent to all this. For the typical say PLG startup, in your experience, do you find folks should hire more of a marketing person than a growth person that focuses on say, conversion or optimizing the funnel or SEO or paid or anything like that? What's your experience there?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你刚聊了增长 PM 这个角色，跟这一切相邻。对典型的 PLG 初创来说，根据你的经验，你觉得大家应该招更多偏向营销的人，还是一个专注在比如转化、漏斗优化、SEO、付费之类的增长型的人？你那边是什么经验？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: For PLG I think you want to have a marketer that is responsible for getting people into the product, that's a marketing profile. That's using all of these channels that's driving inbound, that's focused on web conversion, making sure your website converts, that's a marketing skillset. Because it's really likely you have to work with to get this done is really how I think about it. And you have to work with the people that own the website which is marketing for all of these sort of inbound stuff you are going to work with a lot of people on the marketing team. So that piece is really a marketing piece.
turns.zh: 对 PLG，我觉得你需要一个市场人员负责把人带进产品，那是营销画像。那是用所有这些渠道、驱动入站、聚焦网页转化、确保你的网站能转化——那是营销技能。因为真的，你得跟人协作才能完成这个，我是这么想的。而你必须跟拥有网站的人协作，网站就是营销——所有这些入站的事，你会跟营销团队很多人协作。所以那块真的是营销的活。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: The product experiments and the product test, that's a person with a product skill set because they know how to work with other PMs, they know how to work with engineers and marketers don't. And then there's these gray areas like the onboarding experience or when you first get into the product. And that is an area where there needs to be a ton of collaboration. So my view is that if you're going to have a growth PM, it's probably helpful for them to have EM experience or product experience, but they should be paired as soon as they can be with someone that also understands that top of model piece.
turns.zh: 产品实验和产品测试，那是需要有产品技能的人，因为他们知道怎么跟其他 PM 协作、知道怎么跟工程师协作，而市场人员不知道。然后还有些灰色地带，比如上手体验、或者你刚进产品那会儿。那是一个非常需要大量协作的领域。所以我的看法是：如果你要有一个增长 PM，他们最好有工程经理（EM）经验或者产品经验，但他们应该尽快跟一个也懂那块漏斗顶部的人配对。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Or maybe that person isn't in a full-time growth role, but know who on the marketing team is going to work with them on these areas of crossover like onboarding or that first use experience. And making sure that the signup flow from filling out something on the website to getting in the product is really consistent. Because that area of I'll fill out a handoff, we talk about the marketing to sales handoff all the time on the go to market side, but there's a marketing to product handoff. And that's the handoff that's really important in PLG. And that feels weird to a user, it's two different teams inside of a company.
turns.zh: 或者也许那个人不是全职增长角色，但要知道营销团队里谁会在这些交叉领域——比如上手、或者首次使用体验——跟他们配合。并且确保从在网站上填表到进产品这个注册流程是真正一致的。因为我们聊走向市场时总说营销到销售的衔接，但其实有个营销到产品的衔接。而那在 PLG 里才是真正重要的衔接。对用户来说那感觉会很怪，那是公司里两个不同的团队。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: But if that that feels weird to a user, you're going to notice that all of a sudden feels extremely disjoined. Or if I'm getting a bunch of product transactional emails while I'm getting a bunch of marketing drip emails. So that handoff or that experience needs to be ironed out or consistent or there needs to be tons of collaboration there. So however that is done, I don't really care what the teams look like. Lots of different companies have different versions of how they do this. But the idea is that experience needs to feel consistent and you need to have collaboration across people that have those skill sets and you need to have a clear process for how that looks.
turns.zh: 但如果那对用户来说感觉很怪，你会突然注意到一切变得极其割裂。或者如果我一边收到一堆产品事务性邮件、一边又收到一堆营销 drip 邮件。所以那个衔接、那个体验需要被理顺、要一致，或者那里需要大量的协作。所以不管怎么做，我其实不在乎团队长什么样。很多不同的公司有不同的版本。但核心在于：那个体验需要感觉一致，你需要让拥有这些技能的人之间有协作，你需要有个清晰的流程来定义它长什么样。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And so it's just getting that marketing sales handoff in my opinion. It's like how do you get the marketing to product handoff right? And if it means you have someone that owns onboarding, it's in a hybrid role, then great. If it means there's a committee sort of situation with one person at the DRI, that's great too. So I think my answer is, I don't think there's one way to structure it, it's just highly dependent on the company overall. And I think you need both skill sets.
turns.zh: 所以我的看法就是，把营销到销售的衔接做好——其实就像你怎么把营销到产品的衔接做对？如果这意味着你有个拥有上手体验的人、是个混合角色，那很好。如果这意味着有个委员会式的结构、但有一个人是 DRI（直接责任人），那也很好。所以我的答案是：我觉得没有一种唯一的结构方式，就是高度取决于公司整体。而且我觉得两种技能你都需要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You touched on an area of tension that often comes up between marketing and product. I imagine many listeners hear you saying, marketing should own the website and conversion and net flow. And thinking about the idea of product led growth. The idea that is product will grow our business and oftentimes PMs do that work and oftentimes they're really good at it. And so I guess the question is, in your experience, do you find that it should be marketing more than product or product people?
turns.zh: 你刚才点到了营销和产品之间经常出现的紧张地带。我想很多听众听到你说"营销应该拥有网站、转化和注册流"，再联想到产品驱动增长这个概念——即产品会增长我们的业务，而且 PM 经常做这活、而且常常做得很好。所以我想问的是：根据你的经验，你觉得这应该更归营销、还是更归产品的人？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is it depending on the person, maybe they're called the product person, but they actually are really good at marketing. Any insights there? And then we're going to talk about just collaboration between the two functions.
turns.zh: 是看人吗？也许他们叫产品人，但其实很擅长营销。这方面有什么洞察？然后我们再来聊两个职能之间的协作。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So I think that product led growth is a misnomer. I think people will do anything they can possibly do not call marketing marketing. I think we always see this. And so I think that product led growth really means not as much sales, which means product plus marketing. And so that's probably a hot take. But product led growth is just another name for what we like. I mean, product led growth is a little different than premium or sales server, these things. But you are being handheld by the product, you aren't being handheld by the sales team.
turns.zh: 我觉得产品驱动增长（PLG）是个误称。我觉得人们会使出浑身解数、就是不愿把营销叫成营销。我们总是看到这个。所以我觉得产品驱动增长真正的意思是没那么多销售，也就是产品加营销。所以这可能是个有点冒犯的说法。但产品驱动增长其实就是我们喜欢的东西的另一个名字。我的意思是，产品驱动增长跟免费版或者销售驱动这些有点不同。但你是由产品领着走的，不是由销售团队领着走的。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So really to me, and you can have a sales assist with product led grow as well. But typically what's more at odds in my mind is product led growth means you are going to have a huge sales team early on. It doesn't mean you're not going to have a huge marketing team early on. In fact, to me it means you are going to have a bigger marketing team early on because you're not going to have those sales. Sales is not communicating with customers. So I think it comes back to what are these teams typically good at? And marketing is typically good at the communication piece of one to many. That's what they're good at.
turns.zh: 所以对我而言，你也可以在产品驱动增长里配销售助攻。但通常在我脑子里更对立的是：产品驱动增长意味着你早期不会有一个庞大的销售团队。它并不意味着你早期不会有一个庞大的营销团队。事实上，对我而言它意味着你早期会有一个更大的营销团队，因为你没有那些销售。销售是不跟客户沟通的。所以回到：这些团队通常擅长什么？营销通常擅长一对多的沟通那块。那是他们擅长的。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And so they're usually good. They should be good at figuring out all the channels to have a funnel to communicate with people. And product is really using product as a channel by which to communicate with customers prospects, et cetera. So that's one way of thinking about the difference. On conversion, conversion also means lots of different things. There's top of funnel conversion, getting on the website and filling out some other form. There's conversion once you're in the product becoming an active user or inviting people. So it's like, well, which part of conversion? Web conversion, I typically think of something that's owned by marketing because usually product doesn't want to own the website.
turns.zh: 所以他们通常擅长、也应该擅长想清楚所有渠道、建一个漏斗来跟人沟通。而产品是真的把产品当成渠道，来跟客户、潜在客户等等沟通。所以这是思考差异的一种方式。说到转化，转化也意味着很多不同的东西。有漏斗顶部的转化，就是上网站、填个表。有进到产品之后变成活跃用户、或者邀请别人的转化。所以就像：哪一部分转化？网页转化，我通常认为是营销拥有的，因为通常产品不想拥有网站。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Early on products will sometimes own the website because marketing wasn't there. But the website is something that's going to need to be updated like 5,000 times and it needs to be on Webflow preferably at this point or DMS that's easy update. And if it's built into the code base that's like it, or it's on a headless CMS or it's not touchable by marketing, that's a huge problem. When it comes to once they click the signup button, who should be mostly involved in that process? I think again, there needs to be, I think there's lots of ways to handle that.
turns.zh: 早期产品有时会拥有网站，因为那时候还没营销。但网站这种东西得更新个大概五千次，它最好现在就放在 Webflow 上、或者容易更新的 CMS 里。如果它是写死在代码库里的、或者是用了 headless CMS、营销碰不了，那就是个大问题。说到他们一点注册按钮之后，谁应该主要参与那个流程？我觉得再说一遍，得有——我觉得有很多方式处理这个。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And I think if it's product it kind of has that skillset and the testing skillset and there's enough volume that you can be doing a bunch of tests, maybe that's the person that owns that. But I think there's still going to be a lot of collaboration on the exact words that are used and things like that. So I think it's just whatever it is, make it clear where the handoff is. And so maybe it's not marketing on the entire website because maybe they don't own those flows, but there's this gray area. And I think the other big thing is sometimes the forms, the literal forms that are used are built in your website and sometimes they're built in the product.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果是产品有那个技能、也有测试技能、而且量足够大让你能做一堆测试，也许那就是拥有它的人。但我觉得在用什么具体措辞这类事上，还是会有大量协作。所以我觉得不管是什么，把衔接点划清楚。也许不是营销拥有整个网站，因为也许他们不拥有那些流程，但那里有个灰色地带。我觉得另一个大点是：有时那些表单——字面意义上的表单——是建在你网站里的，有时是建在产品里的。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And I think that also drives a lot of it because it's who do you need to help you build these things? And if they're built into the product, then the product team needs to own that. But it shouldn't to me like this, let's not argue about it, we're trying to move this and here's the things that marketing is going to do and here's the things that product is going to do, and here are the areas of overlap. But I don't think products should be in the business of owning the whole website and all the top of funnel messaging and all of that stuff. That's not the best use of anyone's time really.
turns.zh: 我觉得这也驱动了很大一部分，因为：你需要谁帮你建这些东西？如果它们建在产品里，那产品团队就得拥有它。但对我说来不该是这样——咱们别吵这个，我们要推动这个往前走，这是营销要做的、这是产品要做的、这是重叠的区域。但我不觉得产品该去拥有整个网站、以及所有漏斗顶部的 messaging 等等。那真的不是任何人时间的最好用法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you had a lot of success with marketing and product working together at Asana, and kind of double clicking on the same thread. What have you seen to be an important part of this collaboration and making one plus one equal three, when product and marketing and working together at a B2B company?
turns.zh: 我知道你在 Asana 时营销和产品配合得很好，而且我们刚就同一根线深挖了一下。你看到过，在 B2B 公司里产品和营销一起协作、做到一加一等于三，这个协作里重要的部分是什么？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And look like there were definitely ups and down marketing working with product at Asana as well. But I think overall we did a good job because of some of the systems that Asana had in place. Which is and we talked about this before but something that Asana did well is they had this list in Asana of course, everything at Asana was in Asana through Asana by Asana. But we had a list of areas of responsibility which is just who owns what, it's not your job title. It's what are the things that you are the DRI for? It doesn't mean you're not going to collaborate with people on those things. So what are you the directly responsible individual for?
turns.zh: 而且你看，在 Asana 营销跟产品协作肯定也有起有伏。但我觉得整体我们做得不错，是因为 Asana 有些系统性的东西在。这个我们之前聊过——Asana 做得好的一点是，他们在 Asana 里有一份清单，毕竟 Asana 的一切都是通过 Asana、由 Asana 来管的。但我们有一份"责任领域（AOR, areas of responsibility）"清单，就是谁拥有什么，这不是你的职位头衔。而是：哪些事你是 DRI（直接责任人）？这不意味着你不会跟别人在这些事上协作。所以你到底是哪个"直接责任人"？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And this made it really easy to know who to go to. I'm just going to use DRI because I can't keep saying directly responsible individuals. So the DRI on tests on the onboarding experience is Jennifer the PM. But the copywriter for that is, I don't know, I'm sure who think of exactly who the person was, is Devin on marketing. So we broke it down that's simply so you knew who to go to. Because often what happens with product is they're like, I'm doing a launch, I don't know, especially when there's 15 marketers, I don't know if I'm supposed to go for this product launch or to figure out if this is a launchable feature, so I'm just going to skip it.
turns.zh: 这让"该找谁"变得特别容易。我就直接用 DRI 了，因为"directly responsible individual"我实在说不利索。所以上手体验相关测试的 DRI 是 PM Jennifer。但那块的文案是——我记不清具体是谁了——是营销那边的 Devin。所以我们把它简单拆开，你就知道该找谁。因为产品常发生的情况是：我要做个发布，但我不知道——尤其当有 15 个市场人员时——我该为这个产品发布去找谁、或者该去搞清这是不是个可发布的特性，所以我就干脆跳过了。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So it's really helpful to say the product marketer owner for this part of the product is this and to just have this list. So just having clear ownership is what this comes down to. But it's one thing to have clear ownership but it's quite another to for other teams to know who that clear owner is. So I think having a clear list beyond titles and just like who owns what is really helpful. And then as you hire new people, you can break down those, the list kind of gets longer because you're going to break things down more. It goes from Emily owning all of marketing to me breaking that down and not owning all of it.
turns.zh: 所以，说清楚"这块产品的产品营销负责人是某某"，并且就有这么一份清单，特别有帮助。所以归根结底就是要有清晰的归属。但有清晰归属是一回事，别的团队知道那个清晰的归属者是谁又是另一回事。所以我觉得有一份超越头衔、直接列"谁拥有什么"的清单特别有帮助。然后随着你招新人，你可以把这些拆得更细，清单也就会变长。从"Emily 拥有整个营销"，到我去把它拆开、不再拥有全部。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So I found that really helpful. I also found at Asana we did something called Roadmap Week, which was before every quarter. Where we had of open meetings, sometimes they were open and sometimes they weren't. But we had cross-functional meetings to help plan for what you were going to do that quarter on your team. So I could sit in on the product road mapping for X as the head of marketing. And that was really helpful to just get a sense for what was going on. And sometimes there'd be people in those that were silent participators, and then adopting that would be made so you could see this.
turns.zh: 所以这个我真的觉得很有帮助。我还发现，在 Asana 我们做过一个叫"路线图周（Roadmap Week）"的东西，在每个季度之前。我们有一些公开会议，有时公开、有时不公开。但我们有跨职能的会议，来帮你规划你团队那个季度要做什么。所以作为营销负责人，我能旁听某个产品 X 的路线图制定。那对了解正在发生什么特别有帮助。有时候那里会有些"沉默参与者"，然后采用的情况会被记录下来，这样你就能看到。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And maybe it doesn't scale forever, but it worked really well early on for people being able to be looped on things, to have these sort of out loud landing meetings where you were talking through here are our biggest decisions. Here's what we're wrestling between and getting input, kind of knowing what was going on. I think another thing that we did well was also having clear review processes. And all of this sounds like a lot of process, but once you actually make an AORs list, it kind of runs itself. Someone new gets hired, they're excited to put in their AORs or someone gets the new responsibility and they're stoked to take it over from the head of marketing or whatever it is.
turns.zh: 也许它不能永远规模化，但早期它运作得特别好，让人们能被拉进（looped in）各种事里，有这些"说出来的落地会议"，你在里面讲：这是我们最大的几个决策、这是我们在哪几个选项间纠结、并收集意见，大致知道在发生什么。我觉得我们做得好的另一件事，是还有清晰的评审流程。这一切听起来像很多流程，但一旦你真的把 AOR 清单做出来，它基本就自己转了。招了新人，他们很兴奋地把自己的 AOR 填进去；或者有人接了新责任，他们也很激动从营销负责人手里接过来之类的。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I finally have handed you the master managing editor AOR and it becomes a big deal. The other thing that I think we did well from a marketing perspective is another newsletter that I have is this framework that I use called the GACCS or the GACCS. Which GACCS sounds more fun to say than the GACCS. But this is just a marketing brief that I recommend you do before you make anything big in marketing or do any big projects. And it's just what are the goals? What's the audience? What's the creative or unique end goal? What's this thing? I guess what's going to make it different and stand out from other companies?
turns.zh: 我终于把那个"主编（master managing editor）"的 AOR 交给你了，这就成了一件大事。从营销角度我们做得好的另一件事——我另一份通讯里有个我用的框架，叫 GACCS。这其实就是一份营销简报（brief），我建议你在营销里做任何大事、或者任何大项目之前都做一份。就是：目标（Goals）是什么？受众（Audience）是谁？创意或独特的终极目标（Creative）是什么？这个东西到底是什么？我猜，是什么会让它跟别的公司不一样、脱颖而出？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: The second C is the channels or how this is going to be distributed. How are you going to get the word out about this? Deep thinking there. And then the last few are the stakeholders. Who's the DRI and who needs to weigh in and who's going to be the helper? Who are the contributors? And that's where you can include some product people and you can share this before you start doing any work. So for instance, if you're doing a product launch, product manager communicates with the marketing team. Maybe you have a meeting, maybe you share some brief from the product guide or you share sort of what's being built.
turns.zh: 第二个 C 是渠道（Channels），也就是这个要怎么分发。你打算怎么把这个消息传出去？得在那儿深度思考。然后最后几个（字母）是利益相关方（Stakeholders）。谁是 DRI，谁需要表态，谁会是帮手？谁是贡献者？这就是你能把一些产品的人拉进来的地方，而且你可以在开始做任何事之前就分享这个。比如你要做一个产品发布，产品经理跟营销团队沟通。也许你们开个会，也许你分享产品指南里的一些简报，或者你分享正在被构建的东西。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And then marketing comes back to you with the GACCS. And you can kind weigh in on, here are the channels that are going to be using. The creative C has maybe the highest level messaging. And you get buy in early on and then you can go much faster. And then you're not just sharing with product, here's a blog post that I wrote for the launch. And you're like, what? This is the wrong audience, the wrong thing. You just save so much time sharing these types of things up front. So I find there's a handful of different practices that need to be in place, but it's sharing the right information at the right level of information at the right times and having a culture of doing that.
turns.zh: 然后营销带着 GACCS 回来找你。你可以表态：这是我们要用的渠道。创意那个 C 里可能有最高层的 messaging。你早期就拿到认可（buy-in），然后你就能跑得快得多。然后你就不会只是事后甩给产品说"这是我为发布写的博客文章"。然后产品说：啥？这受众不对、东西也不对。你提前分享这类东西，能省下太多时间。所以我发现需要落实几套不同的实践，但核心就是：在对的时间、以对的信息颗粒度，分享对的信息，并且形成一种这么做的文化。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And it needs to go both ways. Product needs to loop marketing and they are like, here's what we're working on this quarter here are going to be some of the things that we're launching or any of these interesting that you want to double down on and do what public launch for or whatever it is. Or we really think onboarding needs to be approved. Let's put together a group that's going to work on this quarter and let's kind of have a spring plan that's cross-functional. It's a lot of that. So a lot of this happens in a planning process. So if you as a company don't have a good planning process, you're not going to have good cross-functional collaboration, especially between product and marketing.
turns.zh: 而且这得是双向的。产品得把营销拉进来，说：这是我们这季度在做的、这些是我们要发布的一些东西、或者有没有什么有趣的你想重点加码、做个公开发布之类的。或者：我们真的觉得上手体验需要被重视。咱们组个小组这季度一起搞，搞个跨职能的冲刺计划。很多都是这种。所以很多这类事发生在规划流程里。所以如果你们作为一家公司没有好的规划流程，你就不会有好的跨职能协作，尤其是产品和营销之间。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And I think the last thing is just a respect for the skillset. Recognizing you are good at this or you have access to engineers, you know how to get them to do things. I don't want to do that as a marketer. I'm good at storytelling and I know how to get people in the door in the funnel. And let's respect what each person is good at and let them go do their thing. So those are just some of the tactical practices and things that we did in Asana that I thought worked well. But it's hard.
turns.zh: 我觉得最后一点，就是对各自身技能的尊重。意识到你擅长这个、或者你能接触到工程师、你知道怎么让他们做事。作为市场人员我不想干那个。我擅长讲故事，也知道怎么把人从漏斗口引进来。咱们尊重每个人擅长的，让他们去干自己的事。所以这些只是我们在 Asana 做的一些、我觉得运作良好的战术性实践和做法。但这挺难的。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I mean, everyone wants the other team to be doing something a little bit differently and that's always going to be the case. And those tensions in some cases are good because that's why you have the benefit of having different teams and different perspectives. But it gets out of hand when people are just working in silos and aren't communicating with each other, aren't looping people in on things that they're experts on.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，每个人都希望另一个团队做事情的方式稍微不一样点，这永远都会发生。而且有些情况下这些张力是好的，因为那正是你有不同团队、不同视角的好处所在。但当人们只是各自在孤岛里干活、不互相沟通、不把专家拉进他们擅长的事里，那就不受控制了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. All the templates and frameworks that you mentioned we're going to link to in the show notes. One of the things I love about is you're like a PM minded marketer where you make everything super concrete and templated and assigned.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到的所有模板和框架，我们都会在节目备注里链上。我喜欢你的一点是，你像个有 PM 思维的市场人员，把一切都做得特别具体、有模板、有指派。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I like a framework, I like a framework and I like a template. And I am pretty PM minded because I'm pretty well rounded when it comes to the marketing skillset. I don't really consider myself a growth marketer or a product marketer or a content marketer. I just consider myself a marketer who builds teams and that's a different mindset. And I also love goals and planning. No, I don't love annual planning processes that companies do and overdone OKR exercise. It's where you're making this crazy cascade that then nobody can follow.
turns.zh: 我喜欢框架，我喜欢框架，也喜欢模板。而且我很有 PM 思维，因为我在营销技能上是比较全面的。我不太把自己当成增长营销、或者产品营销、或者内容营销。我就把自己当成一个搭团队的市场人员，那是一种不同的心态。而且我也爱目标和规划。不，我可不爱公司做的那种年度规划流程、还有那些过度设计的 OKR 练习。就是那种你搞出一堆疯狂的瀑布式拆解、然后谁都跟不上的东西。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: But basic sort of simple planning so that you kind of go a little slower up front so then you can just fly out getting things out the door. That's the kind of teams I like to lead.
turns.zh: 但那种基础的、简单的规划——让你前期稍微慢一点，然后你就能飞快地往外推出东西。那就是我喜欢带的团队类型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: It's like upfront buy in and then move back, do what you need to do.
turns.zh: 就是前期拿到认可，然后退回去，做你需要做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the sound of that. We're also working on a guest post that may come out before this comes out or after around a lot of this templates. So I'm excited to get that out the door. Coming back to this kind of tension that often happens between PMs and marketing people. Tell me if you agree, but I find that product teams are always often very skeptical of marketing and find that there's just all this time, energy, resources put into marketing efforts. And it's hard to measure who knows what's happening there.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个说法。我们也在写一篇客座文章，可能在节目上线之前或之后发，主题就是这些模板里的很多内容。我很期待把它推出来。回到 PM 和市场人员之间经常出现的那种张力。告诉我你同不同意——我发现产品团队总是很怀疑营销，觉得投入营销的时间和精力、资源太多了。而那里发生了什么很难衡量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: While the product continues to evolve, you can tell what it's doing. It's often driving most of the growth. And so my main question here is, as a product person, what tells you that the marketing person and team is good and awesome and you should trust them and they know what they're doing, versus maybe they're not amazing and we should try to push back? Any advice there?
turns.zh: 而产品一直在演进，你能看出它在做什么。它经常驱动了大部分增长。所以我主要的问题是：作为产品的人，什么会告诉你那个市场人员和团队是好的、厉害的、你该信任他们、他们知道自己在做什么，而不是说他们可能没那么厉害、我们应该推回去？这方面有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah, I recently did a talk with my friend Jenny, who was the head of content at Asana and now is the head of content in Palms at Clear Lake. And she was sort of joking. We were coming up for the name of the talk and she was like, "I want to call it content splatergy versus content strategy." And I was like, "We'll work that in, but maybe that won't be the title, splatergy is really weird word." But it's true. But I think it's funny because a lot of what marketing is that splatergy not strategy, meaning it's just like you just throw a bunch of stuff out there.
turns.zh: 对，我最近跟我朋友 Jenny 做了个演讲，她是 Asana 的内容负责人，现在在另一家公司做内容负责人。她有点开玩笑。我们在想演讲名字，她说："我想叫它'内容乱喷（content splatergy）'对'内容策略（content strategy）'。"我说："我们可以把它揉进去，但也许那不会是标题，splatergy 这词真的怪。"但这是真的。我觉得好笑，因为很多营销做的就是那种 splatergy 而不是 strategy，意思是你就把一堆东西甩出去。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And if you're doing a bunch of work and it's like a lot of busy work and you want to look busy, but it's not impact focus. The best marketing teams are impact focus. They can tell you of all the things they're doing, what are the core things that are of driving that linear growth or just keeping the lights on. They can tell you what their big bets are. What are the things that we are doing right now that we believe can cause step change, top of the funnel growth? Or step change growth on signups or whatever it might be? What are those things? What are the big bets that you're taking? And then what are the foundational pieces of marketing that aren't done yet that might be taking up time?
turns.zh: 而如果你在做一堆活、像是很多忙活、你想显得很忙，但它不是聚焦影响的（impact-focused）。最好的营销团队是聚焦影响的。他们能告诉你，在他们做的所有事里，哪些是驱动那条线性增长、或者只是维持运转的核心事。他们能告诉你他们的大赌注（big bets）是什么。我们现在做的哪些事，我们相信能带来阶跃式变化、漏斗顶部的增长？或者在注册数上带来阶跃式增长？那些是什么？你在下什么大赌注？还有哪些还没做完、可能在占用时间的基础性营销工作？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: We would love to be able to move faster here, but we're like, we don't have a good lead scoring system or we're working on this. We need to redo our website and here's why we need to get it into Webflow and then we'll be able to move faster. So they should be able to break down. Here are the core things we have to do. We're measuring that the core work is working by these TBIs and it's sort of a full funnel view. And we are working on these big bets and here's the foundational things that are broken. So if you ask a marketing lead and you're like, What are their big bets? And they're like, I don't know.
turns.zh: 我们很想能在这儿跑得更快，但我们的情况是，我们还没有好的线索打分系统、或者我们正在搞这个。我们需要重做网站、这是为什么我们需要把它弄进 Webflow、然后我们就能跑更快。所以他们应该能拆开讲。这是我们必须做的核心事。我们在用这些 KPI 衡量核心工作在起作用，而且是个全漏斗的视角。我们在做这些大赌注，而那些破损的基础性东西在这。所以如果你问一个营销负责人：你们的大赌注是什么？他们说：我不知道。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: You can't grow at the rate of venture back startups, you grow by just continuing to do incremental things. That's the same as product I would imagine as well. So they need to have this sort of framework going on. And the other thing that I think is a sign that you're not being impact focused or you're not being effective as a marketing team is this is my favorite thing to pick on And I see it all the time. And I understand why it happens, but don't do it. If our goal is to write 10 blog posts this month. And I'm like, no, that's not a goal, that's maybe a tactic. But the goal should be traffic and the conversion rate from that traffic or the signups that come from that.
turns.zh: 你没法以风投支持的初创那种速度增长，你只能通过持续做增量式的事来增长。我想产品那边也一样。所以他们需要有这种框架在运转。我觉得另一个表明你不是聚焦影响、或者作为营销团队不有效的信号——这是我最爱挑的一点，我老看到。而且我理解它为什么会发生，但别那么做。"如果我们的目标是这个月写 10 篇博客。"我就说：不，那不是目标，那也许是个战术。但目标应该是流量、以及来自那流量的转化率、或者来自那的注册数。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So you shouldn't have activity goals, you should have impact goals. And so the best marketing teams are focused on these funnel metrics. They're not just focused on a certain number signups or qualified leads. They're focused on that number plus maintaining or improving the conversion rate that comes after it. So they're focused on signups with a conversion rate to activated user of the same or better than it is now. Because I can get a lot more people to sign up for a product, but they might be really shitty quality. So you need to have sort of that other threshold. So these are some of the things that I look at to say, is marketing team impact focused?
turns.zh: 所以你不该有"活动目标"，你该有"影响目标"。所以最好的营销团队聚焦在这些漏斗指标上。他们不只盯某个注册数或合格线索数。他们既盯那个数，也盯维持或改善它之后的转化率。所以他们聚焦的是：注册数，加上一个"转化到激活用户"的转化率，跟现在一样或更优。因为我能让更多人注册一个产品，但他们质量可能真的很差。所以你需要有那个另一道门槛。所以这些是我用来判断"营销团队是否聚焦影响"的一些东西。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And when I talk to companies or work with marketers and look at what are they doing and what are their projects, these are the things I usually point out. You need to be more impact focused and here's what you need to do. So that's the big thing that's like are they doing a bunch of busy work or are they doing a bunch of things that can actually lead to tangible growth and what metrics are they using to track that? The other thing is if they're not tracking to my point about not just looking at the raw numbers at each stage of the funnel, but looking at the conversion rates.
turns.zh: 而当我跟公司聊、或者跟市场人员合作、看他们在做什么、他们的项目是什么，这些通常就是我会指出的。你需要更聚焦影响，这是你需要做的。所以那个大问题就是：他们是在做一堆忙活，还是在做一堆真能带来切实增长的事、以及他们用什么指标来追踪？另一件事是：如果他们不追踪——回到我说的，不只看漏斗每个阶段的原始数字，而是看转化率。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: If they're not looking at conversion anywhere at all, there's a huge problem. Because again, I can throw a bunch of people into a funnel stage but they don't convert to the next one, it might not be helping anything. So their focus on conversion not just at the stage of the funnel that they own, but throughout the entire funnel, I think also is a good indicator on if they're being successful as marketers or not.
turns.zh: 如果他们根本任何地方都不看转化，那就是个大问题。因为再说一遍，我可以把一堆人灌进漏斗的某个阶段，但他们不转化到下一阶段，那可能一点用都没有。所以他们聚焦转化的程度——不只看自己拥有的那个漏斗阶段，而是贯穿整个漏斗——我觉得也是判断他们作为市场人员成不成功的一个好指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, these are great. I feel like everything you're saying is music to every PM's ears. That great marketing people should be impact focused, have clear goals in KPIs. You also talked about how it's important to DRIs, like who is responsible for what, being really clear about that, communicating really clearly and often. And then there's this piece about just setting the foundations, like a strong foundation that helps make all these other things successful. This is great.
turns.zh: 对，这些都很棒。我觉得你说的每句话都是每个 PM 爱听的。好的市场人员应该聚焦影响、有清晰的目标和 KPI。你也聊了 DRIs 有多重要——谁负责什么，要把这个说清楚、并且沟通得既清晰又频繁。然后还有这块：打地基，一个强地基能帮所有这些别的事成功。这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine every PM would be like, This is exactly what I want from my marketing team. And your point here is, if your marketing team and lead is not doing these things well, maybe there's an issue and maybe it's not the right marketing person.
turns.zh: 我猜每个 PM 都会说：这正是我对我的营销团队想要的。而你的点是：如果你的营销团队和负责人没把这些事做好，也许就有问题了，也许那个人不是对的营销人。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah. And look, if it's not the team lead, because sometimes you do have, especially at a larger company, you have a team lead that's either on the, you could have someone that's extremely sort of creative and on the brand side of things. But they need to have someone that's working with them that is really good at all of this stuff. It's almost like we need marketing PMs then those tend to be the product marketers or the lead. Because there's so many different projects going on and lots of different things happening. And it's hard to put it all together and say, what are we doing as a marketing team that's moving the needle.
turns.zh: 对。而且你看，如果不是团队负责人——因为有时代价是，你确实会有，尤其在大公司，你有个团队负责人，要么是在……你可能会有个极度偏创意、偏品牌那一侧的人。但他们需要一个跟他们配合、并且在所有这些事上都很厉害的人。这几乎像是我们需要营销 PM，而那通常就是产品营销或者负责人。因为有太多不同的项目在同时进行、太多不同的事在发生。要把它拼到一起、说出"作为营销团队，我们在做什么能推动指针（moving the needle）的事"，很难。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: But I think the other thing about communicating often, it's also communicating at the right level. I find that marketers, even though they're often good at communicating with the audience, they're not good at communicating internally. And I think I've struggled here too as they move to leading larger teams and being on executive teams which is like, what level of information do you need to communicate? And you need to educate people about what marketing does. Because one, marketing often has a bad reputation and so you need to be like, here's what we're actually doing and moving.
turns.zh: 但我觉得关于"频繁沟通"的另一件事，是也要在"对的层级"沟通。我发现市场人员，虽然他们通常擅长跟受众沟通，但他们不擅长内部沟通。而且我觉得我自己往带领更大团队、进高管团队那方向走的时候，也在这儿挣扎过——你需要沟通的信息到底是哪个层级？而且你需要教育别人营销是做什么的。因为一来，营销经常名声不好，所以你需要像这样：这是我们实际在做、并且在推动的事。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And two, there's a lot of jargon in marketing and you got to separate that out and communicate the right level of information at the right time. So I think that's hard too. And so that's why I like things like the DAXs framework and other things like that. And what exactly am I communicating about and at what level. It's hard to get right there too.
turns.zh: 二来，营销里有很多行话，你得把它剥开、在对的时机沟通对的信息层级。所以我觉得那也挺难的。所以这就是为什么我喜欢像 GACCS 框架、以及类似的东西。我到底在沟通什么、在哪个层级。在那儿也很难做对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. One last question before we get to our very exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 太赞了。在进入超激动的快问快答之前，最后一个问题。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I can't wait.
turns.zh: 等不及了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've been waiting all week. So you mentioned that you're a full-time investor basically at this point and the newsletter is a part of that. You've become a really active angel investor and it's really cool to have seen the way you've turned your experience in this really smart way of getting into great deals and supporting founders. And so I'm curious if you have any advice for folks that are thinking about becoming angel investors in the future, just how to leverage their expertise to become successful in investing.
turns.zh: 你等了整整一周了。你刚提到你基本上现在是个全职投资人，通讯是其中一部分。你已经成了个非常活跃的天使投资人，而且能看到你用一种很聪明的方式，把你的经验转化成了拿到好 deal、并且支持创始人，这真的很酷。所以我很好奇，你对那些未来想成为天使投资人的人有没有什么建议——就怎么利用自己的专长、在投资上取得成功。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I think there's a big need for investors that have functional expertise. In traditional VCs. They don't necessarily, maybe they founded companies, maybe they've always been investors or sometimes VC and they really come from sales roles or PM roles. But for me and for marketing and maybe for some of the roles of other people are in, there's not a lot of investors or even advisors from that function and they need help there. And so I think more and more founders are seeing, instead of having advisors or even hiring someone at a function early, it's like, let me lean on angel investors for that.
turns.zh: 我觉得非常有需求的是有职能专长的投资人。传统 VC 里。他们不一定——也许他们创过业、也许他们一直是投资人、或者有时 VC 来自销售角色或者 PM 角色。但对我来说、对营销、也许对其他人所在的某些职能来说，来自那个职能的投资人甚至顾问都不多，而他们在那需要帮助。所以我觉得越来越多创始人发现：与其找顾问、甚至早期在某个职能招人，不如靠天使投资人来补这个。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And so I make it very clear when I talk to founders, this is how I'm going to help. I'm going to help you build your marketing function. I'm definitely going to help you hire, or I'm going to help you shape the job description of the process. I'm probably going to refer you some candidates. I might even refer the candidate that you hire which has happened a bunch of times. And then I'm going to work with that person to make sure that they're setting the right strategy and doing the right things. And so being that clear on here's my exact value add is incredibly helpful.
turns.zh: 所以我在跟创始人聊的时候把话说得很清楚：这就是我会帮忙的方式。我会帮你搭建你的营销职能。我肯定会帮你招人、或者帮你塑造招聘流程和职位描述。我大概率会给你推荐一些候选人。我甚至可能推荐你最后招的那个人——这种事已经发生过好多次了。然后我会跟那个人一起工作，确保他们定的是对的战略、做对的事。所以把"我确切的价值贡献是什么"说清楚，极其有帮助。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And I mean, we get into every deal that we want to. We being I have a business partner named Kathleen, that I do all this with and we can get into any deal. Which I think as an early angel investor, I'm like, why are people saying it's hard to get into a deal? I don't have this problem. And that's not me tapping myself on the shoulder. It's just showing there's huge shortage here. So your skillset might be really valuable to founders and even if you feel like, I don't understand how everything works at a company or things like that, your skillset could be really valuable and they might not see it.
turns.zh: 而且我的意思是，我们能进到每一个我们想进的 deal。"我们"指的是我有个叫 Kathleen 的业务伙伴，所有这些都跟她一起做，而我们能进任何 deal。我觉得作为早期天使投资人，我会想：为什么人们说进 deal 很难？我可没这问题。这不是我在自吹。只是说明这里短缺得很厉害。所以你的技能对创始人可能真的很有价值，哪怕你觉得自己不太懂公司里一切是怎么运转的、之类的，你的技能可能很有价值、而他们可能看不出来。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: It's also when you have a unique skill set and a unique way that you help well articulated. We're going to help you build marketing, it's easy to understand. It makes me easier for other people to bring you into deals. Versus here's another generalist investor that's just going to help. So it's almost like you got to product market yourself. What's the product that you're offering? And then it's so easy, you know Lenny to bring me into deals where they might need some marketing help and there's tons of investors that do that which gets us to deal flow that we need.
turns.zh: 而且当你有一个独特的技能集、以及一个被很好地表达出来的、独特的帮助方式——"我们会帮你搭营销"，这很好理解。这让我更容易被别人带进 deal。而不是"又来一个通才投资人、就那么帮帮忙"。所以这几乎像你得像产品营销自己一样：你提供的"产品"是什么？然后这就太容易了——Lenny，你很清楚什么时候把我带进那些可能需要些营销帮助的 deal，而有大量投资人是这么做的，这就给我们带来了需要的 deal flow。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So I just think if you have a niche or you have an area where you're particularly skilled, you can really leverage that into being a sought after angle. Now, if that makes you a good investor, I'm not sure, there's lots of other things you need to get up to speed on to actually be a good investor. But from the standpoint of helping founders and getting into deals, that can be really helpful.
turns.zh: 所以我只是觉得，如果你有个细分领域、或者有个你特别擅长的方面，你真的可以把那个杠杆化、变成一个人人争抢的天使。现在，这是否让你成为一个好投资人，我不确定——要成为一个真正好的投资人，你还得在好多别的事上跟上节奏。但从帮助创始人、进 deal 的角度，那真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And the other part is you actually have to deliver because then people share more deals with you. And as I said earlier, I've heard so often how helpfully you've been to founders and so that's an important element.
turns.zh: 太棒了。另一块是你真的得交付（deliver），因为那样别人才会跟你分享更多 deal。而且像我之前说的，我老听大家说你对创始人有多有帮助，所以那是个重要因素。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah, you definitely have to deliver. And again, I think that's where it's really helpful to say where you're going to deliver. So they're not necessarily expecting you to deliver on every little thing. They're expecting me to help them hire their marketer, hire contractors in marketing, fill in gaps until they have the marketing team that they need. And so they know when to come to you and then you respond. I think that's also like when people have full-time jobs, I think it's hard to be able to do that full-time jobs that aren't this, it's hard to be able to just tap in and do this kind of stuff.
turns.zh: 对，你绝对得交付。再说一遍，我觉得把"你会在哪交付"说清楚特别有帮助。所以他们不必然期待你在每件小事上都交付。他们期待我帮他们招市场人员、招营销合同工、在他们拥有需要的营销团队之前填补空缺。所以他们知道什么时候该来找你、然后你回应。我觉得另一点是：当人们有全职工作、而那工作不是这个，就很难能随时插进来干这种事。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So it's like don't go overboard because your reputation really, really matters and that's how we've always seen it. We want to be the most helpful angel investors or now we have a small client, but the helpful sort of most helpful investors that you have in your cap table regardless, not just within marketing but within everything. And we do that because we can go really deep on an area and we're always responsible on those areas. And it's good to hear it's working because that's what we're trying to do is be really, really helpful.
turns.zh: 所以别做过头，因为你的声誉真的、真的很重要，而那一直是我们看到的样子。我们想成为最有帮助的那些天使投资人——或者现在我们有一个小基金，但不管怎样，是我们股东席上最有帮助的投资人，不只在营销、而是在所有事上。我们这么做是因为我们能在一个领域挖得很深，并且在那些领域总是负责任的。而且听到这运作得不错很好，因为那正是我们想做的——真的、真的有帮助。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And the other thing too, the last thing I'll say on that is each founder probably thinks, maybe they don't, that it takes us a lot more time than it actually does to be helpful in that area. I had the same conversations over and over again about how to hire a marketer. I can do it in my sleep. So me having that conversation with you and dropping knowledge that you haven't heard, this is what I do all day. But it feels really new because they don't have a lot of people talking to them about marketing. We just have a bunch of candidates that we talk to and our newsletter generates candidates that we talk to.
turns.zh: 还有我最后想说的另一件事：每个创始人也许不觉得，但他们可能以为我们在那个领域帮忙花的时间，比实际多得多。关于怎么招市场人员，我一遍又一遍地聊同样的话。我闭着眼都能做。所以我跟你聊这些、抛出你没听过的知识——这就是我整天在干的事。但对他们来说感觉很新，因为他们没多少人跟他们聊营销。我们只是有一堆我们在聊的候选人，我们的通讯也会产生我们在聊的候选人。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: So anyone can go on our website and get on our list of candidates that we're referring. I talk to one or two candidates a week from that to just meet more marketers. So I have a list of marketers I can refer and say, it's really easy when clients ask me for referrals. So it starts to scale pretty well if you have that niche where you help.
turns.zh: 所以任何人都能上我们网站、进我们推荐的候选人名单。我每周跟其中一两个候选人聊，就为了多见些市场人员。所以我手里有一份可以推荐的市场人员名单，客户找我要推荐时，这就特别轻松。所以如果你有那个你帮忙的细分领域，它就开始相当好地规模化了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I was actually going to add that it may sound scary to feel like you commit to all these startups as an investor, you have to help founders all day. I can say I've invested over 150 companies at this point, which on the surface could feel overwhelming. Like holy shit, all these founders are probably asking you for advice all the time. But I find it's not that, most founders just leave me alone, I'm good.
turns.zh: 对，我其实想补充：作为投资人去承诺帮所有这些初创、整天帮创始人，听起来可能挺吓人。我可以说我到现在投了 150 多家公司，表面上看可能让人崩溃。像"天哪，所有这些创始人可能一直在找你要建议"。但我的发现是并不是那样——大多数创始人就让我清静着，我挺好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or maybe once a quarter, here's something I could really use help with. But it's not as much time as you think and when it is it's really powerful, but it's not an overwhelming amount of time commitment.
turns.zh: 或者也许一个季度一次，"有件事我真的需要帮忙"。但它花的时间没你想的那么多，而一旦花时间，就真的很有力量；但它不是那种压倒性的时间投入。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: The other thing there too is if you refer someone that a company hires, they're going to lobby you forever. You remember that because you sit there and you look at that, I mean, you're maybe not anymore looking at them in an office, but you see and are aware of them every day. And you remember, they came from this person. So one of the most valuable things you could do is refer candidates. And so that's where I think you can add a ton of leverage. You're just referring the right people. So if you have a network and a bunch of people that you know in a certain area like that scenario where you can really do a lot of good for a startup.
turns.zh: 还有那儿的另一个点：如果你推荐了一个人被公司招了，他们会永远念你的好。你记得那个，因为你坐在那儿看那个——我的意思是，你也许不在办公室里看他们了，但你每天都能看到、意识到他们。你记得：他们是那个人介绍来的。所以你能做的最有价值的事之一，就是推荐候选人。所以我觉得那才是你能加上大量杠杆的地方。你只是在推荐对的人。所以如果你有个人脉网络、有一堆你在某个领域认识的人，就像那个场景，你能真的为一家初创做很多好事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Speaking of doing good, we've reached our exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 绝对。说到做好事，我们到了激动人心的快问快答环节了。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Oh, great.
turns.zh: 哦，太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I'm just going to ask you five questions real quick. Whatever comes to mind, let me know. First question, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to people?
turns.zh: 我就快速问你五个问题。想到什么说什么，告诉我。第一个问题：你最常推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I like the classic marketing book, maybe because I think if they're not a classic and they're recency based, marketing changes so fast, like most things in startups and technology. It changes so fast that I like the things that have stood the test of time. And those are things like The Tipping Point and Crossing The Chasm. And I like Seth Godin's Purple Cow, which is just having something that makes you stand out. So those are the classic marketing books and I think every marketer or some of them should have read at some point. I think April Dunford's Obviously Awesome is sort of becoming one of those books that every marketer should have read on positioning.
turns.zh: 我喜欢经典营销书，也许因为我觉得如果它们不是经典、而是基于近期热度的，营销变化太快了——就像初创和科技里大多数东西。它变得太快，所以我喜欢那些经受住时间考验的东西。比如《引爆点》（The Tipping Point）和《跨越鸿沟》（Crossing The Chasm）。我还喜欢 Seth Godin 的《紫牛》（Purple Cow），就是要有让你脱颖而出的东西。所以这些是经典营销书，我觉得每个市场人员、或者至少其中一些，应该在某个时候读过。我觉得 April Dunford 的《Obviously Awesome》正在变成那种每个市场人员都该读过的、讲定位的书。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: It's really helpful even if you're not a product marketer doing positioning, I think it's really helpful. And then the book I read most recently is not related to marketing at all. I read is my partner's favorite book and she was always like, I don't think you're going to like this book, I don't think you'll like it, but it's her favorite book. And it's All The Light We Cannot See about World War II which is of a depressing topic giving all of the tumultuousness in the world. But I thought it was just a very beautifully written book.
turns.zh: 即使你不是做定位的产品营销，它也真的很有帮助，我觉得。然后我最近读的那本书，跟营销完全没关系。我读的是我伴侣最喜欢的书，她一直说：我觉得你不会喜欢这本书，我觉得你不会喜欢，但那是她最喜欢的书。是《我们看不见的光》（All The Light We Cannot See），讲二战的，考虑到这世界所有的动荡，这是个挺让人沮丧的主题。但我觉得它写得真美。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And when you read a lot of business writing a lot, it's kind of nice to step back and just read really beautiful pros on a really heavy topic that isn't just startup marketing. So it was kind of fun to go back and read sort of a older book that was really beautifully written. Next one, Lenny.
turns.zh: 而且当你读了很多商业写作之后，退一步、只读些关于沉重主题、又不是初创营销的、真正优美的散文，挺舒服的。所以回过头读一本写得真美的老书，还挺有趣的。下一个，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question, okay. What's a favorite podcast for you?
turns.zh: 下一个问题，好。你最喜欢的播客是哪个？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Besides yours, obviously. No, I mean, you're doing a great job for someone who's just started off doing podcast. You go deep with people which I think is good, it's not just the service level stuff. Look like the podcast I listen to most is like every night when I go to sleep, I listen to The Daily, the New York Times Daily just gets me to know what's going on. I also like some true crime podcasts but I won't talk about that because maybe that's a little embarrassing and basic. And I think for just getting understanding founders and startups over the years, I found How I Built This to be really helpful.
turns.zh: 除了你的，显然。不，我是说，你作为一个刚开始做播客的人，做得很好。你跟人聊得很深，我觉得这很好，不只是那种表面功夫。我听最多的播客，基本是每晚睡觉前听《The Daily》，纽约时报的 Daily，就让我知道在发生什么。我也喜欢一些真实犯罪播客，但我不聊那个，因为那可能有点尴尬、也有点俗。而且我觉得就理解创始人和初创这些年来说，我发现《How I Built This》真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And I think the main thing I learned from How I Built This is that most startups are really happy. And so if you feel at the beginning if you feel like, we're are just a mess, we're doing everything wrong, that's kind of common. So it's helpful in that regard too. It's like, it's not just me. But I think there's really interesting founder story and hearing how things are built is always helpful. So those are some that I like.
turns.zh: 我觉得我从《How I Built This》学到的主要一点是：大多数初创都真的乱。所以如果你一开始觉得"我们一团糟、我们什么都做错了"，那挺常见的。所以在这方面它也很有帮助。就像：不止我一个。但我觉得那些真正有趣的创始人故事、听东西是怎么建起来的，总是有帮助。所以那些是我喜欢的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的电影或剧？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: My favorite TV show from this year was Yellowjackets on Showtime, which is kind of Lord of the Flies, which had a bunch of women. Lord of the Flies meets lost. It's really good. So it has Christina Ricci in it, the person who was in Casper and now in [inaudible 01:03:14] if you were a girl that grew up in the late 80s and 90s, you will know who Christina Ricci is, or a guy, any gender. I really liked Yellowjackets. I think it's great.
turns.zh: 我今年最喜欢的剧是 Showtime 的《Yellowjackets》，有点像《蝇王》（Lord of the Flies），但主角是群女人。《蝇王》遇上《迷失》。它真的很好。里面有 Christina Ricci，就是演《鬼马小精灵》（Casper）的那个，现在在[听不清]——如果你是个在 80 年代末 90 年代初长大的女孩，你会知道 Christina Ricci 是谁，或者男孩也行、任何性别。我真的很喜欢《Yellowjackets》。我觉得它很棒。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And it was the first show in a while that I've been watching it where I like for the first couple of episodes, I wasn't on my phone half the time. So that's like my measure for, is it good? And then the best movie I've seen recently was we watched CODA, which I think it won some Oscars or something.
turns.zh: 而且这是我很久以来看的第一部剧，头几集我居然有一半时间没在玩手机。所以那是我衡量"它好不好"的标准。然后我最近看过最好的电影，是我们看了《CODA》，我觉得它拿了一些奥斯卡什么的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it won best picture.
turns.zh: 我觉得它拿了最佳影片。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Oh, okay. So it wasn't the Oscar. So I'm really original in my picks here. I'm like, I just watched the Oscar Best Picture, I thought it was great. No, but CODA was like, I think I cried, or at least I almost cried.
turns.zh: 哦，好。所以它不是那个奥斯卡。所以我在选片上真的很原创。我就像：我刚看了奥斯卡最佳影片，我觉得它很棒。不，但《CODA》是，我觉得我哭了，或者至少差点哭了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I actually cried. Yes.
turns.zh: 不，我真的哭了。对。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah, it's about a family who can't hear and then their daughter can hear and they become really interested in music. And there's the story of a family and they're a family of fisherman in Massachusetts, which my brother is a clamor in Massachusetts that's his job. Not his only job, but one of his job that he clams. So he doesn't quite have that fisherman vibe, but somewhat relevant. Yeah, really, really good movie.
turns.zh: 对，它讲的是一个听不见的家庭，然后他们的女儿能听见，她对音乐产生了浓厚兴趣。是一个家庭的故事，他们是在马萨诸塞州的渔民家庭，我兄弟在马萨诸塞州就是个挖蛤人——那是他的工作。不是他唯一的工作，但是其中之一的活儿，他挖蛤。所以他不完全有那种渔民的气质，但有点相关。对，真的、真的很好的电影。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that last scene, powerful. Too much, I'm going to start crying.
turns.zh: 而且最后那个场景，太有力量了。太多（情绪）了，我要开始哭了。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: It's a good one, it's a good family story. Lenny is crying right now. He's just in tears remembering the movie CODA. Lenny is going to spend the rest of the day weeping. You won't get a newsletter next week. It's just because he is rewatching CODA.
turns.zh: 它是个好片，是个好的家庭故事。Lenny 现在正在哭。他泪流满面地回忆《CODA》这部电影。Lenny 今天剩下的时间都会在啜泣。你下周收不到通讯了。就因为他重看了《CODA》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's going to be an emotional newsletter. Speaking of that, what's a favorite interview question that you like to ask?
turns.zh: 那会是一封情绪化的通讯。说到这个，你最喜欢的一个面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Oh, there's so many interview questions that I like to ask. I mean, one of the basic interview questions in marketing that I like to ask is just the company that you're working on, what's the product? Why is it better? Who is it for? It's the most basic positioning question you can ask, but a lot of people can't answer it. So that's a good one. And also if you're writing positioning at your company or if you're on marketing your company and you can't tell me what the product is, why it's better, who it's for, go figure that out if that's what the home page of your website should cover. In fact, the hero of your website and so many don't.
turns.zh: 哦，有太多我喜欢问的面试问题了。我的意思是，营销里一个我喜欢问的基础面试问题是：你正在做的公司，产品是什么？为什么更好？给谁用的？这是你能问的最基础的定位问题，但很多人答不上来。所以那是个好问题。而且，如果你在你公司写定位、或者你在做你公司的营销，而你告诉我不了产品是什么、为什么更好、给谁用的，那就去搞清楚——如果那是你网站首页该覆盖的。其实，你网站的 hero 区就该是那个，而太多网站不是。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: A fun question that I like to ask. It's a mix of getting to know you but also seeing how you communicate is describe something, and I didn't come up with this question, but I really like it. Describe something complicated that you know well that others don't and describe it as simply as you can. And it's just interesting to hear what people pick. Most people pick things related to cooking which is really strange. I ask that question every interview for a long time just as the final question because you learn something about people. And so many people pick cooking.
turns.zh: 一个我喜欢的、有趣的问题。它混合了"了解你"和"看你怎么沟通"：描述一样东西，而且这问题不是我想出来的，但我真的很喜欢。描述一样你很懂、但别人不懂的复杂东西，并且尽可能地用简单的话描述它。听人们挑什么来讲，很有意思。大多数人挑跟烹饪相关的东西，这真的很怪。我问那个问题问了很久，每次面试都作为最后一个问题，因为你能从中了解人。太多人选烹饪了。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: And I'm like, that's a good choice because I find cooking really complicated and I have no idea how to do it. So describe these various aspects of cooking to me. But that's always a fun one. There's other questions that I always ask like walk me through a project you've done recently from start to finish and I'm listening for things can you tell me the goal? And can you tell the audience? But those are more boring, so I'll stop there.
turns.zh: 我就说：那是好选择，因为我发现烹饪真的很复杂、而且我完全不知道怎么做。所以给我描述烹饪的各个层面吧。但那个总是很有趣。还有其他我总问的问题，比如"带我从头到尾走一遍你最近做的一个项目"，而我听的是：你能告诉我目标吗？你能告诉我受众吗？但那些比较无聊，所以我到这儿打住。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: What's your favorite interview question Lenny?
turns.zh: Lenny，你最喜欢的面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh no, I'm asking you questions here.
turns.zh: 哦不，这儿是我在问你问题。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I know I wanted to flip the lightning round back on you. Have you ever done your own lightning round?
turns.zh: 我知道，我想把这快问快答反过来扔给你。你做过你自己的快问快答吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I haven't but I'll answer the question I met away. I'm finding the most popular answer to this question is that second one you just gave which is teach me something I don't know. That comes up a lot in these answers.
turns.zh: 我没做过，但我会回答那个我顺带想到的问题。我发现这个问题最常见的答案是你刚给的第二个：教我一样我不知道的东西。在那些回答里这个出现得很多。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah. Teach me something I don't know. This is a variation on teach me something I don't know. Because it's really about how simply can you communicate it. Teach me something you don't know comes across as a little, I don't want to say pretentious, but it's like it's overwhelming.
turns.zh: 对。教我一样我不知道的东西。这是"教我一样我不知道的东西"的一个变体。因为它真正关乎的是：你能把东西讲得多简单。"教我一样你不知道的东西"听起来有点——我不想说装，但就是有点让人压力山大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, I'll add a little flavor to it as they often say, you have a minute to explain something I don't know, something interesting to you. And so it kind of forces you to be simple about it. But I like the framing.
turns.zh: 嗯，我会像他们常说的那样给它加点味道：你有一分钟来解释一样我不知道的、对你来说有趣的东西。所以它某种程度上逼你把它讲简单。但我喜欢这个框架。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah. It's a complicated framing. And then sometimes what I'll do, especially if they're going to be someone that's going to be writing is I'll be like, okay, make it simpler. And then I'll have them describe it to me again simpler. And I've probably done that in one interview, I've probably done it four times. Which that part isn't super fun but it depends on the person. If I think they can handle kind of joking around, make it simpler. And if I think the topic's interesting, of course, and I'll like want to hear about something so over and over again.
turns.zh: 对。这是个复杂的框架。然后有时我会做的——尤其如果他们将是个要写东西的人——我会说：好，再简单点。然后我会让他们再描述一遍、更简单。我可能在一个面试里，大概做了四次。那部分不是特别有趣，但看人。如果我觉得他们能开得起玩笑，就"再简单点"。而如果我觉得话题有趣，当然，我会想一遍又一遍地听点东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah, I mean it's good to have interview questions that maybe teach you something about how they're going to do at the job, but also learn something about the person. And in a way that's not just tell me about yourself.
turns.zh: 对，我的意思是，有那种既能教你点"他们工作上会怎么干"、又能让你了解这个人的面试问题，是好的。而且方式不是那种"跟我说说你自己"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, who else in the industry do you most respect as a thought leader?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，行业里你最尊重的、作为思想领袖的人是谁？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: The word thought leader here is getting me down but I'll answer the first part of your question. As marketers, we love to paint the phrase thought leader. Some of the other marketer that I think are doing interesting things beyond just marketing is Ashley Meyer is someone who is a marketer who also has a fund now. She was comms at Glossier as well as she used to be at Box and things like that. And is big on Twitter, but she's just someone else who is a marketer in return fund manager. So it's always nice to have other people like that to kind of compare notes with.
turns.zh: "思想领袖"这个词在这儿让我有点提不起劲，但我回答你问题的前半部分。作为市场人员，我们爱把"思想领袖"这词挂在嘴边。其他一些我觉得在做有趣的事、而不只是营销的市场人员——Ashley Meyer，她是个市场人员、现在也有个基金。她在 Glossier 做过公关，也曾在 Box 之类的地方待过。她在 Twitter 上很活跃，但她就是另一个"市场人员转基金经理"的人。所以总有像这样的人可以交流、对笔记，挺好。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: I think that Arielle Jackson from First Round is an amazing support system to founders and marketers at startup. So if you're a first round company, she's a great resource and I think she's just a great resource in general. I also think Kevin Lee, the head of Marketing and Oyster, he's an LPN in our fund, he puts out a newsletter and has a full-time job growing a rapidly growing marketing team. So I have a lot of respect. He's coming to speak to the people in a course that I'm running next week. So he's top of mind. But those are some people that come to mind.
turns.zh: 我觉得 First Round 的 Arielle Jackson 对初创的创始人和市场人员是个惊人的支持系统。所以如果你是一家 First Round 投资的公司，她是个很棒的资源，而且我觉得总体上她就是个很棒的资源。我还觉得 Oyster 的营销负责人 Kevin Lee，他是我们基金的有限合伙人，他出一份通讯，同时有份全职工作在带一个快速增长的营销团队。所以我非常尊重。他下周要来我正在带的一个课上讲话。所以他现在在我脑子里。但这些是我想到的一些人。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: But I mean, I have a lot of marketers that I admire. I'm lucky that in our fund we have over 50 marketers so I have a pretty big arsenal of people I can go to just from that as well. So I lean on the people there for a lot of different things.
turns.zh: 但我的意思是，我有很多我欣赏的市场人员。我很幸运，我们的基金里有超过 50 个市场人员，所以我光从那儿就有很大一票人可以去找。所以很多不同的事我都靠那儿的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're probably going to be raising another fund, and I know you try to raise from marketers and so is that true? Anything you want to add there?
turns.zh: 而且你大概要再募一支基金了，我知道你试着从市场人员那儿募资，所以这是真的吗？有什么想补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: If you're a marketer, we have a fund and we allow for lower minimums for marketers. One of my goals is I don't think there are enough marketers who are investors or know how to get into investing. And I know how much founders need marketing help, so love to encourage more people to get involved in investing and can be the on-ramp for that through our fund. So if you're interested in that at all, or a marketer who's interested in angel investing, I'm always happy to have that conversation with you.
turns.zh: 如果你是个市场人员，我们有支基金，而且我们给市场人员更低的起投门槛。我的一个目标是：我觉得做投资人的、或者知道怎么进投资这行的市场人员还不够多。而我知道创始人在营销上多需要帮助，所以我很乐意鼓励更多人参与投资、并且可以通过我们的基金作为入口。所以如果你对此有任何兴趣，或者是个对天使投资感兴趣的市场人员，我随时乐意跟你聊这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Emily, this was everything I was hoping it would be and more. I feel like we've helped a lot of founders understand the fog of marketing and I think we are probably going to help a lot of PMs and marketing people work together a lot more effectively.
turns.zh: Emily，这期完全就是我希望的样子，甚至更多。我觉得我们帮很多创始人理解了营销的迷雾，而且我想我们大概能帮很多 PM 和市场人员更有效地一起工作。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Hopefully. The fog of marketing, marketing is the San Francisco of functions in a company.
turns.zh: 希望如此。营销的迷雾——营销就是公司里那个像旧金山一样老是雾蒙蒙的职能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Karl the marketing fog.
turns.zh: Karl，营销迷雾。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Karl the marketing fog.
turns.zh: Karl 营销迷雾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 两个最后的问题。如果大家想联系你、了解更多，能在哪儿找到你？听众怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Yeah, I am on Twitter and LinkedIn just Emily Kramer, my name, pretty simple. You can find links to the courses that I run, to the newsletter, to our job board, to talking to me about angel investing as a marketer on our website mkt1.co. And that should set you off in the right direction. And we have lots of things going on to help marketers build out their teams and help founders build out their marketing teams. So if that's you and you're in a situation where you're mostly at a B2B company trying to build out marketing, get in touch with me through my website or through Twitter.
turns.zh: 对，我在 Twitter 和 LinkedIn 上就叫 Emily Kramer，我的名字，挺简单。你能找到我开的课程、通讯、我们的招聘板、以及作为市场人员跟我聊天使投资的链接，都在我们网站 mkt1.co 上。那应该能给你指对方向。而且我们有很多事在进行，帮市场人员搭建他们的团队、帮创始人搭建他们的营销团队。所以如果那是你、而你处在一个主要在 B2B 公司、试图搭建营销的处境里，通过我的网站或者 Twitter 联系我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Emily, thank you for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Emily，谢谢你来这儿。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: Thanks for having me. This was really fun and I'm looking forward to also having that guest newsletter come out with you and just getting Lenny Lennyaised. It's a weird phrase, I won't use that again.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请我。这真的很有趣，而且我很期待那篇客座通讯跟你一起出来，还有就是把你 Lenny 化一下。这是个怪词，我不会再用它了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's move on.
turns.zh: 我们继续吧。

turns.speaker: Emily Kramer
turns.en: We're going to move on. All right. Thanks Lenny.
turns.zh: 我们要继续了。好。谢谢 Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, thanks Emily. Thank you so much for listening. turns.zh: 好，谢谢 Emily。非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这有价值，可以在 Apple Podcast、Spotify、或者你喜欢的播客应用上订阅本节目。另外，请考虑给我们评分或者留个评论，因为这真的能帮到其他听众找到这档播客。你可以在 lennyspodcast.com 找到所有往期节目、或者了解更多关于节目的事。下期见。
